extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, experimenters, builders, and general readers interested in electricity, lightning safety, and practical experiments
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and explanatory principles for understanding lightning as electrical matter, protecting buildings and people from lightning, and performing an electrical kite experiment to draw electric fire from clouds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sameness of electric matter and lightning
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments made in electricity first gave philosophers a suspicion that the matter of lightning was the same with the electric matter; experiments obtaining lightning from clouds by pointed rods and testing it have since proved this suspicion to be perfectly well founded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whatever properties we find in electricity are also the properties of lightning; therefore electrical experiments and precautions are applicable to lightning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and behavior of the electric fluid
rubrics_metrics.description: This matter of lightning or of electricity is an extreme subtile fluid, penetrating other bodies, and subsisting in them, equally diffused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When one body has a greater proportion than another it will communicate until proportions equalize, provided distance isn't too great or proper conductors intervene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conductors — metals and water
rubrics_metrics.description: All metals and water are good conductors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These will convey the electric fluid; when the conductor is good and of sufficient bigness the fluid passes through without hurting it. Metal parts of buildings (lead roofs, metal spouts, rods, bolts, hinges, gilding, silvering, bell wires) provide paths for lightning to earth and prevent damage to less-conductive parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-conductors — dry substances
rubrics_metrics.description: Glass, wax, silk, wool, hair, feathers, and even wood, perfectly dry, are non-conductors: that is, they resist instead of facilitating the passage of this subtile fluid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dry materials resist passage of electric fluid and are more likely to be damaged if the fluid must pass through them; adding moisture can make otherwise poor conductors become conductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial conductivity of damp materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Other bodies may become conductors by having some quantity of water in them, as wood and other materials used in building; but, not having much water in them, they are not good conductors, and, therefore, are often damaged in the operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moisture increases conductivity of building materials, which influences paths lightning takes and damages caused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Striking distance
rubrics_metrics.description: The distance at which a body charged with this fluid will discharge itself suddenly ... is different according to the quantity of the fluid, the dimensions and form of the bodies themselves, and the state of the air between them. This distance ... is called the 'striking distance'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until two bodies come within that distance no stroke will be made; presence of intermediate partial conductors (ragged cloud fragments, objects) can bridge the distance and enable a strike.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tall trees and lofty buildings as imperfect conductors
rubrics_metrics.description: Tall trees and lofty buildings, as the towers and spires of churches, become sometimes conductors between the clouds and the earth; but, not being good ones, that is, not conveying the fluid freely, they are often damaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because they are imperfect conductors the fluid passes through and injures them rather than being safely conveyed to earth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metal-roofed buildings and metal spouts to ground prevent damage
rubrics_metrics.description: Buildings that have their roofs covered with lead or other metal, the spouts of metal continued from the roof into the ground to carry off the water, are never hurt by lightning as, whenever it falls on such a building, it passes in the metals and not in the walls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuous metal runs from roof to ground provide safe conveyance for lightning into earth and protect the structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lightning follows best conductor among available paths
rubrics_metrics.description: When this fluid has an opportunity of passing through two conductors, one good and sufficient, as of metal, the other not so good, it passes in the best, and will follow it in any direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial metal parts embedded in walls (bolts, hinges, gilding, silvering, bell wires, bodies of animals) will attract the current away from less-conductive wall material, often causing localized damage where conductors are discontinuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of iron rod placed from highest part to moist earth
rubrics_metrics.description: An iron rod being placed on the outside of a building, from the highest part continued down into the moist earth ... will receive the lightning at the upper end, attracting it so as to prevent its striking any other part, and affording it a good conveyance into the earth, will prevent its damaging any part of the building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rod should be continuous from top to moist earth to divert strikes safely; if the building is large consider multiple rods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper end elevation, tapering, and gilding of rod
rubrics_metrics.description: We elevate the upper end of the rod six or eight feet above the highest part of the building, tapering it gradually to a fine sharp point, which is gilt to prevent its rusting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tall, sharp, non-rusting point both attracts and draws off charge from clouds; gilding prevents corrosion that would reduce effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower end burial and horizontal run to protect foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: The lower end of the rod should enter the earth so deep as to come at the moist part, perhaps two or three feet; and if bent when under the surface so as to go in a horizontal line six or eight feet from the wall, and then bent again downward three or four feet, it will prevent damage to any of the stones of the foundation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deep and offset burial of the rod's lower end reduces chance of injury to masonry by avoiding current passage too near foundation stones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rod diameter and sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: A small quantity of metal is found able to conduct a great quantity of this fluid. A wire no bigger than a goosequill has been known to conduct (with safety to the building as far as the wire was continued) a quantity of lightning that did prodigious damage both above and below it; and probably larger rods are not necessary, though it is common in America to make them of half an inch, some of three quarters or an inch diameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While very small conductors can work if continuous to earth, common practice favors rods ~1/2"–1" diameter; continuity and proper grounding matter more than massive size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fastening rods with iron staples does not divert lightning
rubrics_metrics.description: The rod may be fastened to the wall, chimney &c., with staples of iron. The lightning will not leave the rod (a good conductor) through those staples. It would rather, if any were in the walls, pass out of it into the rod, to get more readily by that conductor into the earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staples do not provide alternate escape; they help secure the rod without undermining its effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple rods for extensive buildings
rubrics_metrics.description: If the building be very large and extensive, two or more rods may be placed at different parts, for greater security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placement at multiple high points reduces the chance of strikes to unprotected portions of the structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long sharp points presented to clouds draw off charge silently
rubrics_metrics.description: Long sharp points communicating with the earth, and presented to such parts of clouds, drawing silently from them the fluid they are charged with, they are then attracted to the cloud, and may leave the distance so great as to be beyond the reach of striking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pointed conductors can discharge cloud fragments and reduce strike probability by lowering local charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazards inside unsecured houses during thunder
rubrics_metrics.description: A person ... in a house not so secured, will do well to avoid sitting near the chimney, near a looking-glass, or any gilt pictures or wainscot; the safest place is the middle of the room ... sitting on one chair and laying the feet up in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid proximity to partial conductors (chimney, mirrors, gilding). Elevating oneself on insulating supports reduces contact with conductive floor/wall paths; avoid metal-luster fixtures suspended by chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mattresses or hammock for safety during thunder
rubrics_metrics.description: It is still safer to bring two or three mattresses or beds into the middle of the room, and, folding them up double, place the chair upon them; ... a hammock or swinging bed, suspended by silk cords equally distant from the walls on every side, and from the ceiling and floor above and below, affords the safest situation a person can have in any room whatever; and what, indeed, may be deemed quite free from danger of any stroke by lightning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insulating bedding or a silk-suspended hammock reduces conduction paths; silk cords and distance from walls/ceiling/floor minimize contact with conductive structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kite experiment construction and procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a small cross of two light strips of cedar ... tie the corners of the handkerchief to the extremities of the cross ... fix a very sharp-pointed wire [to top] rising a foot or more above the wood. To the end of the twine next the hand is to be tied a silk riband, and where the silk and twine join, a key may be fastened. This kite is to be raised when a thunder-gust appears ... the person who holds the string must stand within a door or window, or under some cover, so that the silk riband may not be wet; and care must be taken that the twine does not touch the frame of the door or window.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use silk cloth (to resist tearing when wet), keep the hand-side silk dry (insulation), avoid contact with building frames, and fly during a thunder-gust so the pointed wire draws electric fire from thunder-clouds into the kite and down the string to the key.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wetting of kite and twine enables conduction and collection
rubrics_metrics.description: When the rain has wetted the kite and twine, so that it can conduct the electric fire freely, you will find it stream out plentifully from the key on the approach of your knuckle. At this key the vial may be charged; and from electric fire thus obtained, spirits may be kindled, and all the other electric experiments be performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wetting provides conductive path; the collected charge can be transferred to bottles and used for standard electrical experiments, confirming sameness of electric matter with lightning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small ragged cloud fragments can act as intermediate conductors
rubrics_metrics.description: Small ragged parts of clouds, suspended in the air between the great body of clouds and the earth (like leaf gold in electrical experiments) often serve as partial conductors for the lightning, which proceeds from one of them to another, and by their help comes within the striking distance to the earth or a building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when the main cloud is out of striking distance, intermediate charged fragments can bridge the gap—heightening need for elevated points and continuous conductors.

rubrics_metrics.name: If conductor insufficient it will be damaged or destroyed
rubrics_metrics.description: If the conductor be good and of sufficient bigness, the fluid passes through it without hurting it. If otherwise, it is damaged or destroyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure conductor continuity and adequate cross-section relative to expected discharge; inadequate conductors localize heating and cause destruction.
